personal.tagline: I break AI systems before your users do, then build the ones that don't break.
personal.proofPoint: I hold two roles right now: QA Engineer at SageTeck and AI Engineer at SkilliHire. In the same week I'll stress-test an AI system and build one. Before this I kept a CRM/ATS platform stable for 10,000+ users at RecruitBPM.
personal.bio: I've broken voice assistants mid-sentence, killed CRM logins on a bad connection on purpose, and thrown enough garbage data at a chatbot to watch it forget what year it is. That's not chaos. That's Tuesday. It's also how I built a QA career: assume the app is guilty until proven innocent. Somewhere along the way, "find what's broken" turned into "build what doesn't break." I'm a Software QA Engineer at SageTeck, where I own the quality gate for web and mobile releases. I'm also an AI Engineer at SkilliHire, designing multi-agent systems, RAG pipelines, and vector search backends. Built for production, not demo day. The two sides feed each other. QA taught me to think like the user who ignores every instruction. AI engineering taught me to build systems that survive that user anyway.

_certificationsHowTo: Add entries below. Only name and kind are required. kind is either 'technical' or 'volunteering'. Fill issuer, date, url (the verify/credential link), image, and includes (component courses, for a specialization) when you have them; each renders only if present. Save certificate scans to public/certificates/ and point image at e.g. /certificates/my-cert.png; landscape works best and anything from ~1.4:1 to ~1.9:1 fits the panel without noticeable letterboxing. For Coursera, the certificate image can be pulled straight from https://s3.amazonaws.com/coursera_assets/meta_images/generated/CERTIFICATE_LANDING_PAGE/CERTIFICATE_LANDING_PAGE~CODE/CERTIFICATE_LANDING_PAGE~CODE.jpeg where CODE is the verify code (1772x928). Udemy is the same idea at https://udemy-certificate.s3.amazonaws.com/image/UC-xxxx.jpg where UC-xxxx is the certificate number (1600x1190, so it letterboxes slightly in the 16/10 panel). Both are plain S3 and are not behind the bot protection the parent sites use, so a verify or certificate URL is all that's needed. Bright Network renders its certificate in HTML rather than serving a file, and the page sits behind Cloudflare, so that one has to be saved from a browser by hand. Delete this note when you're done.

experience.description: I work on multi-agent AI systems, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, and vector search backends meant to run in production rather than sit in a notebook. Mostly LangGraph, LangChain, and modern LLMs, wired into frontends people actually use. I help build the ngedu.ai learning platform alongside the core engineering team. Spending the rest of my week in QA changes how I approach it: I want agent flows that handle the failure cases first, so empty retrievals, tool timeouts, and adversarial prompts are dealt with up front instead of patched in after a demo goes sideways.

I own the quality gate for web and mobile releases across AI products, SuiteCRM, and custom full-stack builds. That covers TalkerCRM (an AI voice and chatbot CRM), Sigla Credit (a financial system with heavy API integration), Route Planner, and Bizzotto CRM. Day to day I design exploratory and regression test plans, validate APIs with Postman, and maintain automated regression suites in Selenium WebDriver and Applitools. I build test cases straight from component diagrams, sequence diagrams, Swagger docs, and user workflows rather than from intuition. I also run performance and stress testing for high-volume email and SMS campaigns, and I log defects in Jira with steps clear enough that nobody has to ask me twice.

Led manual and regression testing for a B2B recruitment ATS/CRM used by large companies, keeping it reliable for 10,000+ users on web and mobile. I validated REST APIs, ran functional, regression, and exploratory suites every release, and maintained manual test cases in TestRail for the key flows and their edge cases. I cut bug-resolution time by tightening our Jira and ClickUp workflow, and worked directly with developers to catch problems early rather than at the end.

projects.title: TalkerCRM, AI Voice CRM
projects.category: AI Quality Engineering · QA meets AI
projects.description: I own the quality gate for a CRM you talk to in plain English, where the thing under test gives a different answer every time and "it worked when I tried it" proves nothing.

caseStudy.problem: TalkerCRM lets users speak to SuiteCRM in natural language to create records, update information, and pull insights. That breaks conventional QA in a specific way. There's no single expected string to assert against. Ask for the same thing three ways and you can get three valid answers, plus one that's confidently wrong. Voice piles on its own problems: accents, background noise, people cutting the assistant off mid-sentence, and half-finished commands that no happy-path script would ever produce.
caseStudy.approach: I treated the AI as untrusted input and untrusted output at the same time. Test cases came from the system's own component diagrams, sequence diagrams, and Swagger docs, so coverage followed the real state space instead of whatever I happened to think of that morning. Then I used AI to generate adversarial datasets at volume: malformed phrasing, contradictory instructions, junk payloads, weird entity names. Those went straight at the voice and chat layers. The important part was validating the whole chain rather than the screen. Spoken intent, parsed command, API call, then the actual CRM record. Plenty of flows return a cheerful confirmation while writing the wrong data, and you only catch that if you go look. I also checked the built-in AI agents on daily task flows and pushed on latency, because an assistant that's correct but slow still gets abandoned.
caseStudy.role: QA owner for the AI voice and chatbot features. Test strategy, adversarial dataset design, API and end-to-end validation, and the release call each sprint.
caseStudy.impact: The bugs that only show up under messy real input, the ones a scripted suite never reaches, got caught before release instead of by users. This is also the project where my two halves started compounding, because generating test data at the scale QA needed meant doing AI engineering to get it.

projects.title: ngedu.ai, AI Learning Platform
projects.description: I help build a live Year 0 to 12 learning platform, working on the multi-agent and retrieval side of it with the core engineering team.

caseStudy.problem: Teaching a national curriculum through an LLM is a grounding problem before it's a teaching problem. Content has to land on-syllabus and at the right grade every single time. A plausible-sounding Year 7 science reading that quietly drifts off the curriculum is a defect, not a style note. On top of that, one overloaded prompt can't reliably tutor a student, deliver a lesson, pace the week, and report to a parent.
caseStudy.approach: I help build the agent and retrieval layer. That means multi-agent flows in LangGraph and LangChain where separate agents own separate teaching jobs, and RAG pipelines with vector search backends that keep generated content anchored to syllabus sources. The QA half of my week shows up here constantly. I push for flows that handle their failure cases first, weak or empty retrievals, tool timeouts, students typing nonsense on purpose, and I check outputs for grounding instead of assuming a clean demo will generalise.
caseStudy.role: AI Engineer on the team. I help build the multi-agent flows, RAG pipelines, and vector search backends. The platform architecture and overall ownership sit with the engineering lead, not with me.
caseStudy.impact: Production AI work on a live, paid platform. It's where I learned the difference between an agent that demos well and one that holds up in front of real students.

projects.title: evidence-rag
projects.description: A RAG service with hybrid retrieval, reranking, and citations the model can't skip. Built so an answer without a source has nowhere to hide, on a stack that costs nothing to run.

caseStudy.problem: Most RAG demos retrieve something, hand it to an LLM, and hope. When retrieval comes back weak the model fills the gap with fluent invention and nothing in the pipeline objects. For anything that matters, an ungrounded answer is a correctness bug, and "the model said so" isn't a source. The usual fix is to throw a paid vector database and a hosted reranker at it, which puts grounded retrieval out of reach if you don't have a budget.
caseStudy.approach: I built the retrieval path so it could be checked, not just so it would return something. Hybrid retrieval runs sparse keyword search alongside dense vectors, which matters because the words in a question rarely match the words in the source. A reranking pass then pushes the genuinely relevant chunks up before anything reaches the model. Grounding is enforced rather than requested politely: generation has to attach citations back to retrieved evidence, so an unsupported claim fails visibly instead of sliding through. The whole thing runs on open, free-tier components on purpose, to show the architecture is doing the work and not the invoice.
caseStudy.role: Solo build. Retrieval design, reranking, citation enforcement, and the evaluation I used to confirm answers stayed grounded.
caseStudy.impact: A working reference for the pattern I care most about, which is making hallucination hard by construction. It's the clearest example of my QA instinct showing up in my engineering: build it so the failure mode is difficult, not merely unlikely.

projects.title: Sigla Credit, Financial Workflows
projects.description: Model-based testing across a live credit platform, where a permissions gap or a wrong API reply isn't a cosmetic bug. It's someone's money.

caseStudy.problem: Sigla Credit runs real financial workflows on SuiteCRM with a lot of API integration behind it. Credit systems fail quietly and expensively. A role that can see one record too many. A workflow that advances even though the API call failed. A state transition nobody wrote a case for. Screens times roles times states times API outcomes is far too large a space to cover by writing test cases from memory, and "we tested the main flow" isn't a release signal.
caseStudy.approach: I derived test cases from the system's own artefacts instead of from intuition: component diagrams, flow charts, sequence diagrams, documented user workflows, and the Swagger spec. That kept coverage tied to the real state space. From there I tested full workflows end to end, across screens, the data underneath, API responses, and permission boundaries, and deliberately spent time on the unhappy paths. Dropped connections mid-transaction, roles reaching for records they shouldn't see, malformed API replies. Each sprint I reported bug status and gave the client a straight release-readiness call with the evidence behind it.
caseStudy.role: QA engineer across the credit and sales CRM workflows. Test derivation, execution, API validation, permission testing, and client reporting each sprint.
caseStudy.impact: The team got a defensible view of release readiness every sprint on a product where correctness is financial. It also covered the permission and workflow edge cases that an intuition-driven test plan reliably walks past.
